references.text: Earlier in the same chapter, the women at the tomb were "terrified" (ἔμφοβοι) in a similar way when they met the angels. The same Greek word is used in [ref:Luk 24:5|Luke 24:5] as in verse 37, linking the two reactions together.

When the disciples saw Jesus walking on the water, they thought it was a ghost (φάντασμα) and were afraid ([ref:Mark 6:49-50|Mark 6:49-50]). The situation is parallel: the disciples see Jesus but think they are seeing something supernatural instead of recognizing him.

In [ref:Matt 14:26-27|Matthew 14:26-27], the disciples thought Jesus was a ghost when he came walking toward them on the sea and were startled—a similar reaction of fear and unbelief as in Luke 24:37.

When Zechariah saw the angel in the temple, he was "troubled" (ἐταράχθη). In [ref:Luk 1:12|Luke 1:12], we find the same type of reaction—fear at a supernatural encounter—that characterizes the disciples' response in 24:37.

In the immediately following passage ([ref:Luk 24:38-39|Luke 24:38-39]), Jesus rebukes the disciples for their doubt and fear, urging them to touch him to see that he is real and not a spirit (πνεῦμα). This is the direct follow-up to the reaction in verse 37.

In [ref:Apg 12:15|Acts 12:15], the believers thought it was Peter's angel knocking at the door, not Peter himself. This shows that belief in spirits and angels appearing in human form was widespread, just as the disciples in Luke 24:37 thought they were seeing a spirit.

The shepherds in the fields "were greatly terrified" (ἐφοβήθησαν φόβον μέγαν) when the angel of the Lord appeared to them ([ref:Luk 2:9|Luke 2:9]). Luke repeatedly describes fear as the natural human response to divine revelations.

At the empty tomb, the women were "terrified" (ἐξεθαμβήθησαν) when they saw a young man in white clothing ([ref:Mark 16:5-6|Mark 16:5-6]). Fear at encountering the supernatural in resurrection accounts is a recurring theme.

In [ref:1 Mos 3:10|Genesis 3:10], Adam says he was afraid when he heard God's voice. Fear as a fundamental human response to meeting the divine is a biblical theme that stretches from the creation account to the resurrection narratives.
